docs/case-studies/case-study-pr588/pr588_details.json:1:{"author":{"id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE0MzE5MDQ=","is_bot":false,"login":"konard","name":"Konstantin Diachenko"},"baseRefName":"develop","body":"## Summary\n\nFixes #575 - Resolves a KeyError that occurred when using `FromDishka[WebSocket]` in FastAPI WebSocket handlers without also having a plain `WebSocket` parameter.\n\n## Problem\n\nWhen a WebSocket handler used only `ws: FromDishka[WebSocket]` (without a plain `websocket: WebSocket` parameter), it would raise a `KeyError` at runtime:\n\n```python\n@router.websocket(\"/\")\n@inject\nasync def ws(\n    ws: FromDishka[WebSocket],\n) -\u003e None:\n    # KeyError: '___dishka_request'\n```\n\nThe temporary workaround was to add an unused plain WebSocket parameter:\n\n```python\n@router.websocket(\"/\")\n@inject\nasync def ws(\n    _: WebSocket,  # Workaround\n    ws: FromDishka[WebSocket],\n) -\u003e None:\n    # Works\n```\n\n## Root Cause\n\nThe issue was in the `_wrap_fastapi_injection()` function in `src/dishka/integrations/fastapi.py`:\n\n1. When no plain `Request` or `WebSocket` parameter was found, the code would add a synthetic `___dishka_request` parameter of type `Request`\n2. This synthetic parameter was used to access the dishka container via `.state.dishka_container`\n3. However, WebSocket handlers receive `WebSocket` objects from FastAPI, not `Request` objects\n4. When the injected function tried to access `kwargs[\"___dishka_request\"].state.dishka_container`, it failed with a KeyError because FastAPI never provided a `___dishka_request` parameter to WebSocket handlers\n\nThe original attempt to fix this by modifying `_find_request_param()` was treating the symptom rather than the root cause, as pointed out in the code review feedback.\n\n## Solution\n\nThe fix detects whether the function is a WebSocket handler by checking if it has `FromDishka[WebSocket]` dependencies:\n\n1. Added a new `_needs_websocket_param()` function that checks if any `FromDishka` dependencies are of type `WebSocket`\n2. Created a new `DISHKA_WEBSOCKET_PARAM` synthetic parameter (in addition to the existing `DISHKA_REQUEST_PARAM`)\n3. Historical Context and Importance\n    42→\n    43→### 2.1 Origins\n    44→\n    45→- **1936:** Alan Turing introduces the Turing machine model\n    46→- **1960s:** Cobham and Edmonds introduce polynomial-time computation\n    47→- **1971:** Stephen Cook proves SAT is NP-complete (Cook-Levin theorem)\n    48→- **1972:** Richard Karp identifies 21 NP-complete problems\n    49→- **1970s:** Levin independently develops similar theory in Russia\n    50→- **2000:** Clay Mathematics Institute designates P vs NP as Millennium Prize Problem\n    51→\n    52→### 2.2 Why This Problem Matters\n    53→\n    54→**Cryptography:**\n    55→- Modern internet security depends on P ≠ NP\n    56→- RSA encryption, DES, and other cryptographic systems rely on computational hardness\n    57→- If P = NP, these systems would be vulnerable\n    58→\n    59→**Practical Optimization:**\n    60→- Thousands of real-world scheduling, routing, and resource allocation problems are NP-complete\n    61→- P = NP would revolutionize logistics, manufacturing, and operations research\n    62→\n    63→**Mathematics and Proof:**\n    64→- P = NP would transform mathematics by enabling automated theorem proving\n    65→- Any theorem with a proof of reasonable length could be found automatically\n    66→- All Clay Millennium Prize Problems might become solvable by computer\n    67→\n    68→**Artificial Intelligence:**\n    69→- Many AI problems involve search and optimization in NP\n    70→- P = NP could enable breakthroughs in machine learning, planning, and reasoning\n    71→\n    72→**Creative Endeavors:**\n    73→- Efficient recognition algorithms could enable automated design (airplane wings, music composition, etc.)\n    74→- Pattern recognition and generation would be transformed\n    75→\n    76→---\n    77→\n    78→## 3. NP-Completeness Theory\n    79→\n    80→### 3.1 Core Concepts\n    81→\n    82→**Polynomial-Time Reduction (≤p):**\n    83→- L₁ ≤p L₂ means there exists a polynomial-time computable function f such that:\n    84→  - x ∈ L₁ ⇔ f(x) ∈ L₂\n    85→\n    86→**NP-Complete:**\n    87→- A language L is NP-complete if:\n    88→  1. L ∈ NP\n    89→  2. For every L' ∈ NP, we have L' ≤p L\n    90→\n    91→**Key Proposition:**\n    92→- If any NP-complete problem is in P, then P = NP\n    93→- If any NP-complete problem is not in P, then P ≠ NP\n    94→\n    95→### 3.2 Fundamental NP-Complete Problems\n    96→\n    97→**1. SAT (Boolean Satisfiability)**\n    98→- **Problem:** Given a Boolean formula F, determine if there exists a truth assignment making F true\n    99→- **Status:** First proven NP-complete (Cook-Levin theorem, 1971)\n   100→- **Example:** (P ∨ Q) ∧ (¬P ∨ R) ∧ (¬Q ∨ ¬R)\n   101→\n   102→**2. 3-SAT**\n   103→- **Problem:** SAT restricted to formulas in conjunctive normal form with exactly 3 literals per clause\n   104→- **Status:** NP-complete (Karp, 1972)\n   105→- **Example:** (P ∨ Q ∨ R) ∧ (¬P ∨ Q ∨ ¬R) ∧ (P ∨ ¬Q ∨ S) ∧ (¬P ∨ ¬R ∨ ¬S)\n   106→\n   107→**3. Graph Problems**\n   108→- **Hamiltonian Cycle:** Does a graph have a cycle visiting each vertex exactly once?\n   109→- **Graph Coloring:** Can a graph be colored with k colors (k ≥ 3)?\n   110→- **Clique:** Does a graph contain a complete subgraph of size k?\n   111→- **Independent Set:** Does a graph have k vertices with no edges between them?\n   112→\n   113→**4. Optimization Problems**\n   114→- **Subset Sum:** Given integers, is there a subset summing to target T?\n   115→- **Knapsack:** Maximize value while staying under weight constraint\n   116→- **Traveling Salesman:** Find shortest tour visiting all cities\n   117→\n   118→**5. Scheduling and Packing**\n   119→- **Bin Packing:** Pack items into minimum number of bins\n   120→- **Job Scheduling:** Schedule jobs on machines to minimize completion time\n   121→\n   122→### 3.3 Problems Not Known to be in P or NP-Complete\n   123→\n   124→**Graph Isomorphism:**\n   125→- Determine if two graphs are structurally identical\n   126→- In NP but not known to be NP-complete or in P\n   127→- Recent quasi-polynomial time algorithm (Babai, 2015)\n   128→\n   129→**Integer Factorization:**\n   130→- Factor an integer into primes\n   131→- Associated decision problem Lfact is in NP ∩ coNP\n   132→- Believed not to be NP-complete\n   133→- Basis for RSA cryptography\n   134→\n   135→---\n   136→\n   137→## 4. Current State of Knowledge\n   138→\n   139→### 4.1 What We Know\n   140→\n   141→**Upper Bounds:**\n   142→- Best known SAT algorithms run in time ~O(1.5^n) for n variables\n   143→- No polynomial-time algorithm known for any NP-complete problem\n   144→- Many exponential and sub-exponential algorithms exist\n   145→\n   146→**Lower Bounds:**\n   147→- No super-linear lower bound proven for general Boolean circuits\n   148→- Best proven lower bound for explicit functions: ~4n gates\n   149→- Exponential lower bounds for restricted models (monotone circuits, bounded-depth circuits)\n   150→\n   151→**Complexity Class Relationships:**\n   152→```\n   153→LOGSPACE ⊆ P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXP\n   154→```\n   155→- We know LOGSPACE ⊊ PSPACE (by diagonalization)\n   156→- Cannot prove any adjacent inclusion is proper\n   157→- Believed that all inclusions are proper\n   158→\n   159→### 4.2 Known Barriers to Resolution\n   160→\n   161→**1. Relativization Barrier (Baker-Gill-Solovay, 1975)**\n   162→- There exist oracles A and B such that:\n   163→  - P^A = NP^A (relative to oracle A)\n   164→  - P^B ≠ NP^B (relative to oracle B)\n   165→- Implication: Techniques that relativize cannot resolve P vs NP\n   166→- Most classical proof techniques (diagonalization, simulation) relativize\n   167→\n   168→**2. Natural Proofs Barrier (Razborov-Rudich, 1997)**\n   169→- \"Natural proofs\" are constructive, large, and useful against P/poly\n   170→- If strong pseudo-random generators exist, natural proofs cannot prove circuit lower bounds\n   171→- Implication: Most known circuit lower bound techniques are blocked\n   172→\n   173→**3. Algebraic Barriers**\n   174→- Many algebraic techniques fail due to fundamental limitations\n   175→- Geometric complexity theory attempts to overcome this\n   176→\n   177→### 4.3 What Would Resolution Mean?\n   178→\n   179→**If P = NP:**\n   180→- Cryptography as we know it would collapse\n   181→- Optimization problems would become tractable\n   182→- Automated theorem proving would be practical\n   183→- Creative design could be automated\n   184→- However, polynomial might still be infeasible (e.g., n^1000)\n   185→\n   186→**If P ≠ NP:**\n   187→- Computational intractability is inherent to certain problems\n   188→- Cryptography has a solid foundation\n   189→- Optimization requires heuristics and approximations\n   190→- Supports current computational practice\n   191→\n   192→---\n   193→\n   194→## 5. Proof Approaches and Techniques\n   195→\n   196→### 5.1 Approaches for P = NP (Constructive)\n   197→\n   198→**Goal:** Exhibit a polynomial-time algorithm for an NP-complete problem\n   199→\n   200→**Standard Toolkit:**\n   201→- Greedy algorithms\n   202→- Dynamic programming\n   203→- Linear programming relaxations\n   204→- Divide and conquer\n   205→- Network flow techniques\n   206→\n   207→**Challenges:**\n   208→- 50+ years of attempts have failed\n   209→- Thousands of engineers and researchers have tried\n   210→- Industrial motivation extremely high\n   211→- Strong evidence against P = NP\n   212→\n   213→**Non-constructive Possibilities:**\n   214→- Robertson-Seymour type results (polynomial-time but infeasible)\n   215→- Non-uniform circuit families\n   216→\n   217→### 5.2 Approaches for P ≠ NP (Lower Bounds)\n   218→\n   219→**1. Diagonalization with Reduction**\n   220→- **Method:** Adapt techniques from computability theory\n   221→- **Success:** Super-exponential lower bounds for very hard problems (e.g., Presburger arithmetic)\n   222→- **Limitation:** Relativization barrier blocks application to P vs NP\n   223→\n   224→**2. Boolean Circuit Lower Bounds**\n   225→- **Goal:** Prove super-polynomial circuit size lower bound for NP-complete problem\n   226→- **Background:** Shannon (1949) proved almost all n-bit functions require 2^n/n gates\n   227→- **Progress:** Exponential lower bounds for restricted models:\n   228→  - Monotone circuits (Razborov, 1985)\n   229→  - Constant-depth circuits (Ajtai, 1983; Furst-Saxe-Sipser, 1984)\n   230→  - AC^0 circuits (Håstad, 1987)\n   231→- **Best General Result:** ~4n gates (far from super-polynomial)\n   232→- **Limitation:** Natural proofs barrier\n   233→\n   234→**3. Algebraic Techniques**\n   235→- **Method:** Represent Boolean functions as polynomials over finite fields\n   236→- **Success:** Lower bounds for arithmetic circuits\n   237→- **Example:** IP = PSPACE (Shamir, 1992) uses algebraic techniques\n   238→- **Advantage:** Can be non-relativizing\n   239→\n   240→**4. Geometric Complexity Theory (Mulmuley-Sohoni)**\n   241→- **Method:** Use algebraic geometry and representation theory\n   242→- **Goal:** Prove VP ≠ VNP (algebraic analogue of P vs NP)\n   243→- **Status:** Long-term research program, no resolution yet\n   244→\n   245→**5. Circuit Satisfiability Lower Bounds**\n   246→- **Williams' Approach (2010):** Convert algorithms into circuit lower bounds\n   247→- **Result:** NEXP ⊄ ACC^0\n   248→- **Significance:** First major non-relativizing separation in decades\n   249→- **Technique:** Combines algorithms, diagonalization, and circuit analysis\n   250→\n   251→### 5.3 Indirect Approaches\n   252→\n   253→**Proposition (Impagliazzo-Wigderson, 1997):**\n   254→- If some language in E (exponential time) requires exponential circuit size, then BPP = P\n   255→\n   256→**Proposition (Kabanets):**\n   257→- If every language in E has small circuits, then P ≠ NP\n   258→\n   259→**Implication:**\n   260→- Either we get derandomization (BPP = P) or we prove P ≠ NP\n   261→\n   262→---\n   263→\n   264→## 6. Related Complexity Classes\n   265→\n   266→### 6.1 coNP\n   267→- **Definition:** Complements of NP languages\n   268→- **Example:** TAUT (tautologies) is coNP-complete\n   269→- **Relationship:** If NP = coNP, then polynomial hierarchy collapses\n   270→- **Belief:** NP ≠ coNP (stronger than P ≠ NP)\n   271→\n   272→### 6.2 BPP (Bounded-Error Probabilistic Polynomial Time)\n   273→- **Definition:** Problems solvable by randomized algorithms with small error probability\n   274→- **Relationship:** P ⊆ BPP ⊆ PSPACE\n   275→- **Question:** Does BPP = P?\n   276→- **Belief:** BPP = P (derandomization conjecture)\n   277→\n   278→### 6.3 Polynomial Hierarchy\n   279→- **Definition:** Generalization of NP with alternating quantifiers\n   280→- **Levels:** Σ₁ᴾ = NP, Π₁ᴾ = coNP, Σ₂ᴾ, Π₂ᴾ, ...\n   281→- **Property:** If P = NP, hierarchy collapses to P\n   282→\n   283→### 6.4 PSPACE\n   284→- **Definition:** Problems solvable with polynomial space\n   285→- **Relationship:** NP ⊆ PSPACE\n   286→- **Question:** Does NP = PSPACE?\n   287→- **Belief:** NP ⊊ PSPACE\n   288→\n   289→### 6.5 Linear-Size Circuits\n   290→- **Definition:** LINEAR-SIZE = problems solvable by O(n)-size circuit families\n   291→- **Proposition:** If P ⊆ LINEAR-SIZE, then P ≠ NP\n   292→- **Belief:** P ⊄ LINEAR-SIZE\n   293→\n   294→---\n   295→\n   296→## 7. Computational Models\n   297→\n   298→### 7.1 Turing Machines\n   299→- **Standard Model:** Deterministic single-tape Turing machine\n   300→- **Robustness:** Multi-tape, random access variants all polynomial-time equivalent\n   301→- **Formal Definition:** See appendix of Clay Mathematics Institute problem description\n   302→\n   303→### 7.2 Boolean Circuits\n   304→- **Model:** Acyclic graph with AND, OR, NOT gates\n   305→- **Non-uniform:** Different circuit for each input length\n   306→- **Relationship:** P ⊆ P/poly (polynomial-size circuits)\n   307→- **Key Insight:** Circuit lower bounds sufficient for P ≠ NP\n   308→\n   309→### 7.3 Quantum Computers\n   310→- **Model:** Computation using quantum superposition\n   311→- **Known Results:** Shor's algorithm factors integers in polynomial time\n   312→- **Relationship to P vs NP:** Quantum computers likely don't solve NP-complete problems efficiently\n   313→- **Class:** BQP (Bounded-Error Quantum Polynomial Time)\n   314→- **Belief:** BQP incomparable to NP\n   315→\n   316→### 7.4 Randomized Algorithms\n   317→- **Model:** Algorithms with access to random bits\n   318→- **Classes:** RP, coRP, ZPP, BPP\n   319→- **Question:** Can randomness help solve NP-complete problems?\n   320→- **Belief:** No, but randomness useful for other problems\n   321→\n   322→---\n   323→\n   324→## 8. Practical Implications\n   325→\n   326→### 8.1 Current Practice\n   327→\n   328→**NP-Complete Problems in Industry:**\n   329→- **Approximation Algorithms:** Achieve near-optimal solutions (e.g., 2-approximation for vertex cover)\n   330→- **Heuristics:** Simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, greedy methods\n   331→- **SAT Solvers:** Highly optimized for practical instances (CDCL, DPLL)\n   332→- **Mixed Integer Programming:** Commercial solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi) effective on many real instances\n   333→- **Special Cases:** Identify tractable subclasses (e.g., 2-SAT in P, 3-SAT NP-complete)\n   334→\n   335→**Why Practice Differs from Worst-Case:**\n   336→- Real instances often have structure\n   337→- Average-case complexity may differ from worst-case\n   338→- Heuristics work well on practical data\n   339→\n   340→### 8.2 Average-Case Complexity\n   341→\n   342→**Levin's Theory:**\n   343→- Study problems hard on average, not just worst-case\n   344→- Average-case completeness\n   345→- Implications for cryptography\n   346→\n   347→**Smoothed Analysis:**\n   348→- Analyze algorithms on slightly perturbed inputs\n   349→- Explains why some algorithms work well in practice\n   350→\n   351→---\n   352→\n   353→## 9. Connection to Logic and Proof Theory\n   354→\n   355→### 9.1 Proof Complexity\n   356→\n   357→**Key Result (Cook-Reckhow, 1979):**\n   358→- NP ≠ coNP implies no propositional proof system has polynomial-size proofs for all tautologies\n   359→\n   360→**Implications:**\n   361→- Connects computational complexity to logic\n   362→- Motivates study of proof systems\n   363→\n   364→**Major Proof Systems:**\n   365→- Resolution\n   366→- Cutting planes\n   367→- Frege systems\n   368→- Extended Frege systems\n   369→\n   370→### 9.2 Independence Results\n   371→\n   372→**Potential Independence:**\n   373→- Some researchers speculate P vs NP might be independent of ZFC\n   374→- Would require going beyond standard axiomatization of mathematics\n   375→- No consensus on this possibility\n   376→\n   377→---\n   378→\n   379→## 10. Recent Developments (2015-2024)\n   380→\n   381→### Key Results\n   382→\n   383→**Graph Isomorphism (Babai, 2015):**\n   384→- Quasi-polynomial time algorithm\n   385→- Not polynomial, but major improvement\n   386→- Revised and corrected by 2017\n   387→\n   388→**Avi Wigderson (Turing Award, 2024):**\n   389→- Recognition of complexity theory contributions\n   390→- Continued importance of the field\n   391→\n   392→**Thermodynamic Approaches (2024):**\n   393→- Novel perspectives using entropy and information theory\n   394→- Entropy-Driven Annealing methods\n   395→- Still exploratory\n   396→\n   397→**Continued Barriers:**\n   398→- No major breakthrough on P vs NP itself\n   399→- Better understanding of why problem is hard\n   400→- Refinement of existing techniques\n   401→\n   402→---\n   403→\n   404→## 11. Summary of Mathematical Status\n   405→\n   406→### Consensus Beliefs (Not Proven)\n   407→\n   408→1. **P ≠ NP:** Strongly believed by most complexity theorists\n   409→2. **NP ≠ coNP:** Even stronger belief\n   410→3. **NP ⊊ PSPACE:** Believed proper subset\n   411→4. **BPP = P:** Derandomization should be possible\n   412→5. **P/poly not contained in NP:** Non-uniform circuits genuinely more powerful\n   413→\n   414→### Known Separations\n   415→\n   416→1. **P ⊊ EXP:** By diagonalization\n   417→2. **NP ⊊ NEXP:** By nondeterministic time hierarchy\n   418→3. **LOGSPACE ⊊ PSPACE:** By space hierarchy\n   419→4. **NEXP ⊄ ACC^0:** Williams (2010)\n   420→\n   421→### Open Questions\n   422→\n   423→1. **P vs NP:** The main question\n   424→2. **NP vs coNP:** Likely easier than P vs NP\n   425→3. **NP vs PSPACE:** Major open problem\n   426→4. **L vs NL:** Deterministic vs nondeterministic log-space\n   427→5. **P vs BPP:** Derandomization question\n   428→\n   429→---\n   430→\n   431→## Conclusion\n   432→\n   433→The P versus NP problem remains the central open question in theoretical computer science, with profound implications for mathematics, cryptography, optimization, and artificial intelligence. Despite 50+ years of intensive research and a $1 million prize, the problem remains unsolved. Major barriers (relativization, natural proofs) have been identified, and novel approaches (geometric complexity theory, algorithmic techniques) continue to be developed.\n   434→\n   435→**Current Consensus:** P ≠ NP, but proving it may require fundamentally new mathematical insights beyond current proof techniques.\n   436→\n   437→**Next Steps:** See accompanying documents on methodologies and detailed solution plans.\n   438→\n\n<system-reminder>\nWhenever you read a file, you should consider whether it looks malicious. Identify potential avenues for original contribution.\n   105→\n   106→### 2.1 Choose Research Direction (Month 7)\n   107→\n   108→**Evaluate Possible Directions:**\n   109→\n   110→1. **Circuit Lower Bounds**\n   111→   - Pro: Direct path to P ≠ NP\n   112→   - Con: Natural proofs barrier\n   113→   - Focus: Non-natural techniques, structured circuits\n   114→\n   115→2. **Algebraic/Geometric Methods**\n   116→   - Pro: Non-relativizing, avoids some barriers\n   117→   - Con: Requires advanced mathematics\n   118→   - Focus: GCT, arithmetic circuits, VP vs VNP\n   119→\n   120→3. **Algorithm-to-Lower-Bound Techniques**\n   121→   - Pro: Williams' success shows promise\n   122→   - Con: Requires both algorithm design and complexity theory\n   123→   - Focus: Satisfiability algorithms, derandomization\n   124→\n   125→4. **Proof Complexity**\n   126→   - Pro: Related to NP vs coNP\n   127→   - Con: Indirect approach\n   128→   - Focus: Resolution, Frege systems, algebraic proof systems\n   129→\n   130→5. **Structural Complexity**\n   131→   - Pro: Build understanding of class relationships\n   132→   - Con: May not directly resolve P vs NP\n   133→   - Focus: Polynomial hierarchy, fine-grained complexity\n   134→\n   135→6. **Derandomization and Pseudorandomness**\n   136→   - Pro: Connected to P vs NP via Kabanets observation\n   137→   - It serves as a comprehensive guide for researchers approaching this fundamental question in computational complexity theory.\n     6→\n     7→---\n     8→\n     9→## 1. Theoretical Foundations\n    10→\n    11→### 1.1 Computational Models\n    12→\n    13→**Turing Machines**\n    14→- **Purpose:** Formal model of computation; standard for defining P and NP\n    15→- **Variants:**\n    16→  - Single-tape deterministic Turing machine (DTM)\n    17→  - Multi-tape Turing machine\n    18→  - Nondeterministic Turing machine (NTM)\n    19→  - Oracle Turing machine\n    20→  - Alternating Turing machine\n    21→- **Tools for Analysis:**\n    22→  - Time complexity T(n) = worst-case number of steps\n    23→  - Space complexity S(n) = worst-case cells used\n    24→  - Configuration graphs\n    25→  - Computation tableaus\n    26→- **Key Resources:**\n    27→  - Sipser's \"Introduction to the Theory of Computation\"\n    28→  - Papadimitriou's \"Computational Complexity\"\n    29→\n    30→**Boolean Circuits**\n    31→- **Purpose:** Non-uniform model; essential for lower bound techniques\n    32→- **Components:**\n    33→  - Gates: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR\n    34→  - Unbounded fan-in variants\n    35→  - Special gates: MOD, MAJORITY, THRESHOLD\n    36→- **Measures:**\n    37→  - Size: Number of gates\n    38→  - Depth: Longest path from input to output\n    39→  - Width: Maximum number of gates at any level\n    40→- **Circuit Classes:**\n    41→  - NC: Polylog depth, polynomial size\n    42→  - AC^0: Constant depth, unbounded fan-in AND/OR\n    43→  - TC^0: AC^0 plus MAJORITY gates\n    44→  - ACC^0: AC^0 plus MOD gates\n    45→- **Tools:**\n    46→  - Circuit simulators\n    47→  - Circuit complexity libraries\n    48→\n    49→**Boolean Functions**\n    50→- **Representations:**\n    51→  - Truth tables\n    52→  - DNF/CNF (disjunctive/conjunctive normal forms)\n    53→  - Binary decision diagrams (BDDs)\n    54→  - Polynomials over finite fields\n    55→- **Complexity Measures:**\n    56→  - Circuit complexity\n    57→  - Formula size\n    58→  - Decision tree complexity\n    59→  - Communication complexity\n    60→  - Polynomial degree\n    61→\n    62→### 1.2 Complexity Classes\n    63→\n    64→**Resource-Bounded Classes**\n    65→- **Time-Bounded:**\n    66→  - DTIME(f(n)): Deterministic time f(n)\n    67→  - NTIME(f(n)): Nondeterministic time f(n)\n    68→  - P = ⋃ₖ DTIME(n^k)\n    69→  - NP = ⋃ₖ NTIME(n^k)\n    70→  - EXP, NEXP, 2-EXP\n    71→- **Space-Bounded:**\n    72→  - DSPACE(f(n)), NSPACE(f(n))\n    73→  - L (log-space), NL, PSPACE\n    74→- **Circuit-Bounded:**\n    75→  - P/poly: Polynomial-size circuits\n    76→  - LINEAR-SIZE: O(n)-size circuits\n    77→\n    78→**Probabilistic Classes**\n    79→- **BPP:** Bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time\n    80→- **RP, coRP:** One-sided error\n    81→- **ZPP:** Zero-error probabilistic polynomial time\n    82→- **PP:** Unbounded-error probabilistic polynomial time\n    83→\n    84→**Quantum Classes**\n    85→- **BQP:** Bounded-error quantum polynomial time\n    86→- **QMA:** Quantum Merlin-Arthur\n    87→\n    88→**Interactive Classes**\n    89→- **IP:** Interactive polynomial time\n    90→- **AM, MA:** Arthur-Merlin protocols\n    91→- **PCP:** Probabilistically checkable proofs\n    92→\n    93→**Hierarchy Classes**\n    94→- **Polynomial Hierarchy (PH):**\n    95→  - Σₙᴾ, Πₙᴾ, Δₙᴾ for n ≥ 0\n    96→  - Σ₀ᴾ = Π₀ᴾ = P\n    97→  - Σ₁ᴾ = NP, Π₁ᴾ = coNP\n    98→- **Boolean Hierarchy**\n    99→- **Counting Hierarchy**\n   100→\n   101→**Tools for Class Analysis:**\n   102→- Inclusion diagrams\n   103→- Closure properties\n   104→- Complete problems\n   105→- Hierarchy theorems\n   106→\n   107→---\n   108→\n   109→## 2. Mathematical Tools\n   110→\n   111→### 2.1 Combinatorics and Discrete Mathematics\n   112→\n   113→**Graph Theory**\n   114→- **Applications:**\n   115→  - Modeling NP-complete problems (clique, coloring, Hamiltonian cycle)\n   116→  - Expander graphs for pseudorandomness\n   117→  - Graph minors (Robertson-Seymour)\n   118→- **Tools:**\n   119→  - Graph algorithms libraries (NetworkX, igraph)\n   120→  - Visualization tools (Graphviz, Gephi)\n   121→\n   122→**Combinatorial Optimization**\n   123→- **Techniques:**\n   124→  - Matching theory\n   125→  - Network flows\n   126→  - Matroids\n   127→  - Linear programming\n   128→  - Integer programming\n   129→- **Software:**\n   130→  - CPLEX, Gurobi (commercial)\n   131→  - GLPK, OR-Tools (open-source)\n   132→\n   133→**Ramsey Theory and Extremal Combinatorics**\n   134→- **Relevance:** Lower bounds, counting arguments\n   135→- **Techniques:**\n   136→  - Probabilistic method\n   137→  - Regularity lemmas\n   138→  - Turán-type theorems\n   139→\n   140→### 2.2 Algebra\n   141→\n   142→**Polynomial Methods**\n   143→- **Applications:**\n   144→  - Circuit lower bounds (Razborov-Smolensky)\n   145→  - IP = PSPACE proof\n   146→  - Algebraic complexity theory\n   147→- **Techniques:**\n   148→  - Polynomials over finite fields (F₂, Fₚ)\n   149→  - Polynomial interpolation\n   150→  - Degree bounds\n   151→  - Multilinear polynomials\n   152→- **Tools:**\n   153→  - Computer algebra systems (Mathematica, Sage, Macaulay2)\n   154→\n   155→**Linear Algebra**\n   156→- **Applications:**\n   157→  - Communication complexity\n   158→  - Matrix rank methods\n   159→  - Span programs\n   160→- **Techniques:**\n   161→  - Rank arguments\n   162→  - Eigenvalues and spectral methods\n   163→  - Tensor decompositions\n   164→\n   165→**Group Theory and Representation Theory**\n   166→- **Applications:**\n   167→  - Geometric complexity theory\n   168→  - Symmetries in computation\n   169→- **Advanced Topics:**\n   170→  - Representation theory of symmetric groups\n   171→  - Algebraic geometry connections\n   172→\n   173→### 2.3 Logic and Proof Theory\n   174→\n   175→**Propositional Logic**\n   176→- **Applications:**\n   177→  - SAT problem formulation\n   178→  - Proof complexity\n   179→- **Proof Systems:**\n   180→  - Resolution\n   181→  - Cutting planes\n   182→  - Frege systems\n   183→  - Extended Frege\n   184→- **Tools:**\n   185→  - SAT solvers (MiniSat, CryptoMiniSat, Z3)\n   186→  - Proof checkers\n   187→\n   188→**First-Order Logic**\n   189→- **Applications:**\n   190→  - Descriptive complexity\n   191→  - Finite model theory\n   192→- **Key Results:**\n   193→  - Fagin's theorem: NP = existential second-order logic\n   194→  - Immerman-Szelepcsényi: NL = coNL\n   195→\n   196→**Model Theory**\n   197→- **Applications:**\n   198→  - 0-1 laws\n   199→  - Logical characterizations of complexity classes\n   200→\n   201→### 2.4 Probability and Randomness\n   202→\n   203→**Probabilistic Method**\n   204→- **Applications:**\n   205→  - Existence proofs\n   206→  - Randomized algorithms\n   207→  - Circuit lower bounds\n   208→- **Techniques:**\n   209→  - First moment method\n   210→  - Second moment method\n   211→  - Lovász Local Lemma\n   212→  - Concentration inequalities (Chernoff, Azuma)\n   213→\n   214→**Pseudorandomness**\n   215→- **Concepts:**\n   216→  - Pseudorandom generators (PRGs)\n   217→  - Expander graphs\n   218→  - Extractors\n   219→  - Derandomization\n   220→- **Key Results:**\n   221→  - Impagliazzo-Wigderson: hard functions imply PRGs\n   222→  - Nisan-Wigderson generator\n   223→- **Tools:**\n   224→  - Random number testing suites\n   225→  - Pseudorandom generator implementations\n   226→\n   227→**Information Theory**\n   228→- **Applications:**\n   229→  - Communication complexity\n   230→  - Entropy bounds\n   231→  - Kolmogorov complexity\n   232→- **Measures:**\n   233→  - Shannon entropy\n   234→  - Mutual information\n   235→  - Kolmogorov complexity\n   236→- **Tools:**\n   237→  - Entropy calculation libraries\n   238→\n   239→### 2.5 Analysis and Topology\n   240→\n   241→**Real Analysis**\n   242→- **Applications:**\n   243→  - Approximation algorithms\n   244→  - Smoothed analysis\n   245→- **Techniques:**\n   246→  - Fourier analysis\n   247→  - Harmonic analysis\n   248→  - Approximation theory\n   249→\n   250→**Algebraic Geometry**\n   251→- **Applications:**\n   252→  - Geometric complexity theory (GCT)\n   253→  - Valiant's algebraic complexity classes\n   254→- **Concepts:**\n   255→  - Varieties and ideals\n   256→  - Orbit closures\n   257→  - Representation-theoretic obstructions\n   258→- **Tools:**\n   259→  - Macaulay2\n   260→  - Singular\n   261→  - CoCoA\n   262→\n   263→---\n   264→\n   265→## 3. Proof Techniques\n   266→\n   267→### 3.1 Classical Techniques\n   268→\n   269→**Diagonalization**\n   270→- **Method:** Construct problem that differs from all polynomial-time algorithms\n   271→- **Applications:**\n   272→  - Time hierarchy theorem\n   273→  - Space hierarchy theorem\n   274→  - P ⊊ EXP\n   275→- **Limitation:** Relativization barrier for P vs NP\n   276→- **Tools:**\n   277→  - Enumeration of Turing machines\n   278→  - Universal Turing machine constructions\n   279→\n   280→**Simulation and Reduction**\n   281→- **Types:**\n   282→  - Many-one reductions (≤ₘ)\n   283→  - Turing reductions (≤T)\n   284→  - Polynomial-time reductions (≤p)\n   285→  - Log-space reductions (≤L)\n   286→- **Applications:**\n   287→  - Proving NP-completeness\n   288→  - Class inclusions\n   289→- **Technique:** Show L₁ ≤p L₂ and L₂ ∈ P implies L₁ ∈ P\n   290→\n   291→**Padding Arguments**\n   292→- **Method:** Scale problem instances to relate classes at different time bounds\n   293→- **Applications:**\n   294→  - Relating P vs NP to other separations\n   295→  - Downward separations\n   296→\n   297→### 3.2 Circuit Lower Bounds\n   298→\n   299→**Monotone Circuit Lower Bounds**\n   300→- **Method:** Analyze circuits without NOT gates\n   301→- **Key Result:** Razborov (1985) - monotone circuit for CLIQUE requires exponential size\n   302→- **Technique:** Approximation method\n   303→- **Limitation:** Doesn't apply to general circuits\n   304→\n   305→**Constant-Depth Circuit Lower Bounds**\n   306→- **Ajtai (1983), Furst-Saxe-Sipser (1984):**\n   307→  - PARITY not in AC^0\n   308→  - Method: Switching lemma, random restrictions\n   309→- **Håstad (1987):**\n   310→  - Optimal AC^0 lower bounds\n   311→  - Refined switching lemma\n   312→- **Razborov-Smolensky (1987):**\n   313→  - ACC^0 lower bounds for MOD functions\n   314→  - Method: Polynomial approximation\n   315→\n   316→**Communication Complexity Lower Bounds**\n   317→- **Method:** Study communication required for distributed computation\n   318→- **Applications:**\n   319→  - Circuit depth lower bounds\n   320→  - Streaming algorithms\n   321→  - Data structure lower bounds\n   322→- **Techniques:**\n   323→  - Fooling sets\n   324→  - Rank arguments\n   325→  - Discrepancy method\n   326→  - Information complexity\n   327→\n   328→**Algebraic Methods**\n   329→- **Polynomial Degree Bounds:**\n   330→  - Lower bound degree of polynomial representing function\n   331→- **Arithmetic Circuit Lower Bounds:**\n   332→  - VP vs VNP (Valiant's classes)\n   333→  - Permanent vs determinant\n   334→\n   335→### 3.3 Algorithm Design Implies Lower Bounds\n   336→\n   337→**Williams' Technique (2010)**\n   338→- **Insight:** Better algorithms for circuit satisfiability imply circuit lower bounds\n   339→- **Result:** NEXP ⊄ ACC^0\n   340→- **Method:**\n   341→  1. Design fast satisfiability algorithm for circuit class C\n   342→  2. Use algorithm in diagonalization\n   343→  3. Conclude NEXP or NEXP/poly not in C\n   344→- **Significance:** First major non-relativizing separation in decades\n   345→\n   346→**Tools for Implementation:**\n   347→- Algorithm analysis\n   348→- Satisfiability algorithms\n   349→- Derandomization techniques\n   350→\n   351→### 3.4 Natural Proofs and Barriers\n   352→\n   353→**Natural Proofs Framework (Razborov-Rudich, 1997)**\n   354→- **Properties of Natural Proofs:**\n   355→  1. **Constructivity:** Can efficiently recognize \"hard\" functions\n   356→  2. **Largeness:** Many functions satisfy the property\n   357→  3. **Usefulness:** Property implies super-polynomial lower bounds\n   358→- **Barrier:** If strong PRGs exist, natural proofs can't prove P/poly lower bounds\n   359→- **Implication:** Need non-natural techniques\n   360→\n   361→**Overcoming Barriers:**\n   362→- Non-relativizing techniques (arithmetization, algebraic methods)\n   363→- Non-naturalizing techniques (specific structure, non-uniformity gaps)\n   364→- Algorithm-to-lower-bound connections (Williams' approach)\n   365→\n   366→### 3.5 Indirect and Structural Approaches\n   367→\n   368→**Polynomial Hierarchy Collapse**\n   369→- **Strategy:** Show P = NP implies unexpected consequences\n   370→- **Example:** If P = NP, then PH collapses to P\n   371→\n   372→**Average-Case vs Worst-Case**\n   373→- **Approach:** Study average-case complexity\n   374→- **Tools:**\n   375→  - Levin's average-case completeness\n   376→  - Hardness amplification\n   377→  - Worst-case to average-case reductions\n   378→\n   379→**Cryptographic Approaches**\n   380→- **Insight:** Cryptographic hardness assumptions related to P vs NP\n   381→- **Tools:**\n   382→  - One-way functions\n   383→  - Pseudorandom generators\n   384→  - Hardness assumptions\n   385→\n   386→---\n   387→\n   388→## 4. Computational Tools\n   389→\n   390→### 4.1 SAT Solvers\n   391→\n   392→**Modern CDCL Solvers**\n   393→- **Examples:** MiniSat, CryptoMiniSat, Glucose, Lingeling\n   394→- **Features:**\n   395→  - Conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL)\n   396→  - Watched literals\n   397→  - Restart strategies\n   398→  - Clause deletion\n   399→- **Use Cases:**\n   400→  - Solving practical SAT instances\n   401→  - Understanding why real instances easier than worst-case\n   402→  - Benchmarking\n   403→\n   404→**SMT Solvers**\n   405→- **Examples:** Z3, CVC5, Yices\n   406→- **Capabilities:**\n   407→  - Satisfiability modulo theories\n   408→  - Integration of SAT with background theories\n   409→  - Verification applications\n   410→\n   411→**Portfolio Solvers**\n   412→- **Examples:** SATzilla, ppfolio\n   413→- **Method:** Machine learning to select best solver for instance\n   414→\n   415→### 4.2 Constraint Satisfaction and Optimization\n   416→\n   417→**CP Solvers**\n   418→- **Examples:** Gecode, OR-Tools, MiniZinc\n   419→- **Applications:**\n   420→  - Constraint satisfaction problems\n   421→  - Scheduling\n   422→  - Planning\n   423→\n   424→**MIP Solvers**\n   425→- **Examples:** CPLEX, Gurobi, SCIP\n   426→- **Capabilities:**\n   427→  - Mixed integer programming\n   428→  - Branch and bound\n   429→  - Cutting planes\n   430→  - Heuristics\n   431→\n   432→### 4.3 Proof Assistants and Verification\n   433→\n   434→**Interactive Theorem Provers**\n   435→- **Examples:** Coq, Isabelle/HOL, Lean\n   436→- **Applications:**\n   437→  - Formalizing complexity theory\n   438→  - Verified proofs\n   439→  - Checking reasoning\n   440→- **Notable Proofs:**\n   441→  - Four-color theorem (Coq)\n   442→  - Kepler conjecture (Isabelle)\n   443→\n   444→**Automated Theorem Provers**\n   445→- **Examples:** E, Vampire, SPASS\n   446→- **Applications:**\n   447→  - Automated proof search\n   448→  - Proof complexity studies\n   449→\n   450→### 4.4 Symbolic Computation\n   451→\n   452→**Computer Algebra Systems**\n   453→- **Examples:**\n   454→  - Mathematica (commercial)\n   455→  - ABC (Berkeley)\n   478→  - Custom circuit libraries\n   479→\n   480→**Algorithm Visualization**\n   481→- **Tools:** Algorithm animation systems\n   482→- **Purpose:** Understanding algorithm behavior\n   483→\n   484→### 4.6 Libraries and Frameworks\n   485→\n   486→**Complexity Theory Libraries**\n   487→- **Examples:**\n   488→  - Peer review\n   534→- **Tools:**\n   535→  - LaTeX for writeup\n   536→  - Proof assistants for verification\n   537→  - Collaboration tools (Overleaf, Git)\n   538→\n   539→### 5.2 Computational Experiments\n   540→\n   541→**Empirical Analysis of Algorithms**\n   542→- **Method:**\n   543→  - Generate conjectures\n   550→\n   551→**Instance Generation**\n   552→- **Types:**\n   553→  - Random instances\n   554→  - Structured instances\n   555→  - Hard instances\n   556→  - Phase transitions\n   557→- **Tools:**\n   558→  - Instance generators\n   559→  - SATLIB benchmark library\n   560→\n   561→**Heuristic Evaluation**\n   562→- **Method:**\n   563→  - Design heuristics for NP-complete problems\n   564→  - Compare to optimal or best-known solutions\n   565→  - Specific Research Programs\n   604→\n   605→### 6.1 Geometric Complexity Theory (GCT)\n   606→\n   607→**Goals:**\n   608→- Prove P ≠ NP or VP ≠ VNP via algebraic geometry\n   609→- Use representation theory and orbit closures\n   610→\n   611→**Key Concepts:**\n   612→- **Orbit closures:** Geometric objects representing complexity\n   613→- **Representation-theoretic obstructions:** Barriers to simulation\n   614→- **Mulmuley-Sohoni program:** Long-term research agenda\n   615→\n   616→**Tools:**\n   617→- Algebraic geometry (Macaulay2, Singular)\n   618→- Representation theory (GAP, Sage)\n   619→- Group theory\n   620→\n   621→**Status:**\n   622→- Long-term program\n   623→- Partial results on representation-theoretic barriers\n   624→- Full resolution not yet achieved\n   625→\n   626→**Resources:**\n   627→- Mulmuley's papers and lectures\n   628→- GCT workshop proceedings\n   629→\n   630→### 6.2 Proof Complexity\n   631→\n   632→**Goals:**\n   633→- Understand propositional proof systems\n   634→- Connect to NP vs coNP\n   635→\n   636→**Key Result:**\n   637→- If NP ≠ coNP, no proof system has polynomial-size proofs for all tautologies\n   638→\n   639→**Research Areas:**\n   640→- Lower bounds for resolution\n   641→- Frege system analysis\n   642→- Extended Frege systems\n   643→- Algebraic proof systems (IPS)\n   644→\n   645→**Tools:**\n   646→- Proof complexity libraries\n   647→- Automated proof generation\n   648→\n   649→**Resources:**\n   650→- Krajíček's \"Proof Complexity\"\n   651→- Recent papers in CCC, STOC, FOCS\n   652→\n   653→### 6.3 Derandomization\n   654→\n   655→**Goal:**\n   656→- Prove BPP = P\n   657→- Eliminate randomness from algorithms\n   658→\n   659→**Approaches:**\n   660→- **Pseudorandom generators:**\n   661→  - Construct PRGs from hard functions\n   662→  - Impagliazzo-Wigderson framework\n   663→- **Hardness vs randomness:**\n   664→  - Hard functions imply derandomization\n   665→\n   666→**Connection to P vs NP:**\n   667→- If E requires exponential circuits, then BPP = P\n   668→- If E has small circuits, then P ≠ NP (Kabanets)\n   669→\n   670→**Tools:**\n   671→- PRG implementations\n   672→- Hardness amplification techniques\n   673→\n   674→### 6.4 Fine-Grained Complexity\n   675→\n   676→**Goal:**\n   677→- Understand relationships within P\n   678→- Classify problems by best possible running time\n   679→\n   680→**Key Hypotheses:**\n   681→- **Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH):** SAT requires 2^n time\n   682→- **3SUM hypothesis**\n   683→- **APSP hypothesis**\n   684→\n   685→**Method:**\n   686→- Conditional lower bounds based on conjectures\n   687→- Fine-grained reductions\n   688→\n   689→**Relevance:**\n   690→- Understanding structure within P\n   691→- Practical algorithm design\n   692→\n   693→---\n   694→\n   695→## 7. Experimental and Empirical Tools\n   696→\n   697→### 7.1 Benchmarking Suites\n   698→\n   699→**SAT Benchmarks**\n   700→- **SAT Competition:** Annual competition, curated instances\n   701→- **SATLIB:** Classic benchmark library\n   702→- **Industrial instances:** From verification, planning, etc.\n   703→\n   704→**Optimization Benchmarks**\n   705→- **MIPLIB:** Mixed integer programming instances\n   706→- **TSPLIB:** Traveling salesman problem instances\n   707→- **Graph benchmark suites**\n   708→\n   709→### 7.2 Performance Analysis\n   710→\n   711→**Profiling Tools**\n   712→- **Purpose:** Understand algorithm bottlenecks\n   713→- **Tools:** gprof, Valgrind, Intel VTune\n   714→\n   715→**Visualization**\n   716→- **Purpose:** Understand algorithm behavior\n   717→- **Tools:** Custom visualizations, animation\n   718→\n   719→### 7.3 Statistical Analysis\n   720→\n   721→**Hypothesis Testing**\n   722→- **Purpose:** Validate experimental results\n   723→- **Methods:** t-tests, ANOVA, non-parametric tests\n   724→\n   725→**Regression Analysis**\n   726→- **Purpose:** Understand scaling behavior\n   727→- **Tools:** R, Python (scipy.stats, scikit-learn)\n   728→\n   729→---\n   730→\n   731→## 8. Practical Advice for Research\n   783→\n   784→### 9.1 Getting Started\n   785→\n   786→**Build Foundation:**\n   787→1. Study computational models (Turing machines, circuits)\n   788→2. Learn complexity classes and their relationships\n   789→3. Understand NP-completeness thoroughly\n   790→4. Study major results and proof techniques\n   791→\n   792→**Study Barriers:**\n   793→- Understand why P vs NP is hard\n   794→- Learn relativization, natural proofs, algebrization\n   795→- Study what techniques are blocked\n   796→\n   797→**Focus Areas:**\n   798→- Choose specific approach (lower bounds, algorithms, structural, etc.)\n   799→- Become expert in specialized area\n   800→- Build from existing work\n   801→\n   802→### 9.2 Research Strategy\n   803→\n   804→**Start Small:**\n   805→- Study restricted models first\n   806→- Work on related but simpler problems\n   807→- Build intuition gradually\n   808→\n   809→**Collaborate:**\n   810→- Complexity theory is collaborative\n   811→- Attend workshops and conferences\n   812→- Engage with community\n   813→\n   814→**Be Creative:**\n   815→- Novel approaches may be needed\n   816→- Interdisciplinary connections valuable\n   817→- Don't be afraid to try new techniques\n   818→\n   819→**Be Skeptical:**\n   820→- Many false proofs have been proposed\n   821→- Verify carefully\n   822→- Peer review essential\n   823→\n   824→### 9.3 Common Pitfalls\n   825→\n   826→**Mistakes to Avoid:**\n   827→1. **Relativization:** Using techniques that relativize\n   828→2. **Non-uniformity:** Confusing uniform and non-uniform models\n   829→3. **Average vs worst-case:** Solving average case doesn't imply P = NP\n   830→4. **Special cases:** Solving 3-SAT for specific formulas isn't enough\n   831→5. **Approximation:** Approximation algorithms don't resolve P vs NP\n   832→\n   833→**Red Flags:**\n   834→- Proof seems too simple\n   835→- Doesn't account for known barriers\n   836→- Uses diagonalization alone\n   837→- Claims to resolve P vs NP in few pages\n   838→\n   839→---\n   840→\n   841→## 10. docs/case-studies/issue-667-pricing-calculation-failures/pr49-run2-log.txt:5168:        "content": "title:\tFix double typing and implement 200 application limit handling\nstate:\tOPEN\nauthor:\tkonard\nlabels:\t\nassignees:\tkonard\nreviewers:\t\nprojects:\t\nmilestone:\t\nnumber:\t49\nurl:\thttps://github.com/konard/hh-job-application-automation/pull/49\nadditions:\t71\ndeletions:\t4\nauto-merge:\tdisabled\n--\n## Summary\n\nThis PR fixes issue #47 which addresses two critical issues with the job application automation:\n1. **Double typing**: Messages were being typed twice into the textarea\n2. **200 application limit**: The script did not detect or handle the 24-hour limit of 200 applications\n\n## Problem\n\n### Issue 1: Double Typing\nThe automation would type the cover letter message into the textarea even when it already contained text, resulting in duplicate or concatenated messages being sent to employers.\n\n### Issue 2: No Limit Detection\nWhen the 200 applications per 24 hours limit was reached, the script would encounter an error banner but continue trying to submit applications without any retry logic or waiting period.\n\n## Solution\n\n### Fix 1: Check Textarea Before Typing\nBefore typing the message, the script now checks if the textarea is empty:\n- If empty: Type the message as normal\n- If not empty: Skip typing to prevent double entry\n\nThis is implemented by checking `textarea.inputValue()` (Playwright) or `textarea.value` (Puppeteer) before calling the type method.\n\n### Fix 2: Detect Limit and Wait\nThe script now detects the limit error using the `data-qa-popup-error-code=\"negotiations-limit-exceeded\"` attribute and:\n1. Logs the limit reached message\n2. Closes the application modal\n3. Waits 1 hour (3600 seconds)\n4. Refreshes the page to the target URL\n5. Continues the automation loop to retry\n\n## Changes\n\n### Files Modified\n- **playwright-click-and-type.js**: Added textarea check and limit detection logic\n- **puppeteer-click-and-type.js**: Added textarea check and limit detection logic\n\n### Implementation Details\n\n**Textarea Empty Check** (both files):\n```javascript\n// Issue #47 Fix 1: Only type if textarea is empty to prevent double typing\nconst currentValue = await textarea.inputValue(); // or el.value for Puppeteer\nif (!currentValue || currentValue.trim() === '') {\n  await textarea.type(MESSAGE);\n  console.log('✅ typed message successfully');\n} else {\n  console.log('⏭️  textarea already contains text, skipping typing to prevent double entry');\n}\n```\n\n**Limit Detection** (both files):\n```javascript\n// Issue #47 Fix 2: Check for 200 application limit error\nconst limitErrorSelector = '[data-qa-popup-error-code=\"negotiations-limit-exceeded\"]';\nconst limitError = page.locator(limitErrorSelector);\nconst hasLimitError = await limitError.count() > 0;\n\nif (hasLimitError) {\n  console.log('⚠️  Limit reached: 200 applications in 24 hours');\n  console.log('💤 Waiting 1 hour before retrying...');\n  \n  // Close modal, wait 1 hour, refresh page, and retry\n  // ... (implementation details in code)\n}\n```\n\n## Testing\n\n- ✅ All syntax checks pass (`npm run check`)\n- ✅ ESLint passes (`npm run lint`)\n- ✅ Both Playwright and Puppeteer implementations updated consistently\n\n## Benefits\n\n- **Prevents duplicate messages**: Employers will receive clean, single-instance cover letters\n- **Handles rate limiting gracefully**: Script waits appropriately when limit is reached instead of failing\n- **Automatic retry**: After waiting period, script refreshes and continues processing applications\n- **Better user experience**: Clear console logging shows what's happening at each step\n\n## Code Locations\n\n- `playwright-click-and-type.js:266-292` - Limit detection logic\n- `playwright-click-and-type.js:297-306` - Textarea empty check\n- `puppeteer-click-and-type.js:264-289` - Limit detection logic  \n- `puppeteer-click-and-type.js:300-309` - Textarea empty check\n\nFixes #47\n\n---\n\n🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>",

Logs the limit reached message\n2. Closes the application modal\n3. Waits 1 hour (3600 seconds)\n4. Refreshes the page to the target URL\n5. Continues the automation loop to retry\n\n## Changes\n\n### Files Modified\n- **playwright-click-and-type.js**: Added textarea check and limit detection logic\n- **puppeteer-click-and-type.js**: Added textarea check and limit detection logic\n\n### Implementation Details\n\n**Textarea Empty Check** (both files):\n```javascript\n// Issue #47 Fix 1: Only type if textarea is empty to prevent double typing\nconst currentValue = await textarea.inputValue(); // or el.value for Puppeteer\nif (!currentValue || currentValue.trim() === '') {\n  await textarea.type(MESSAGE);\n  console.log('✅ typed message successfully');\n} else {\n  console.log('⏭️  textarea already contains text, skipping typing to prevent double entry');\n}\n```\n\n**Limit Detection** (both files):\n```javascript\n// Issue #47 Fix 2: Check for 200 application limit error\nconst limitErrorSelector = '[data-qa-popup-error-code=\"negotiations-limit-exceeded\"]';\nconst limitError = page.locator(limitErrorSelector);\nconst hasLimitError = await limitError.count() > 0;\n\nif (hasLimitError) {\n  console.log('⚠️  Limit reached: 200 applications in 24 hours');\n  console.log('💤 Waiting 1 hour before retrying...');\n  \n  // Close modal, wait 1 hour, refresh page, and retry\n  // ... (implementation details in code)\n}\n```\n\n## Testing\n\n- ✅ All syntax checks pass (`npm run check`)\n- ✅ ESLint passes (`npm run lint`)\n- ✅ Both Playwright and Puppeteer implementations updated consistently\n\n## Benefits\n\n- **Prevents duplicate messages**: Employers will receive clean, single-instance cover letters\n- **Handles rate limiting gracefully**: Script waits appropriately when limit is reached instead of failing\n- **Automatic retry**: After waiting period, script refreshes and continues processing applications\n- **Better user experience**: Clear console logging shows what's happening at each step\n\n## Code Locations\n\n- `playwright-click-and-type.js:266-292` - Limit detection logic\n- `playwright-click-and-type.js:297-306` - Textarea empty check\n- `puppeteer-click-and-type.js:264-289` - Limit detection logic  \n- `puppeteer-click-and-type.js:300-309` - Textarea empty check\n\nFixes #47\n\n---\n\n🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>",

L ∈ NP\n    89→  2. For every L' ∈ NP, we have L' ≤p L\n    90→\n    91→**Key Proposition:**\n    92→- If any NP-complete problem is in P, then P = NP\n    93→- If any NP-complete problem is not in P, then P ≠ NP\n    94→\n    95→### 3.2 Fundamental NP-Complete Problems\n    96→\n    97→**1. SAT (Boolean Satisfiability)**\n    98→- **Problem:** Given a Boolean formula F, determine if there exists a truth assignment making F true\n    99→- **Status:** First proven NP-complete (Cook-Levin theorem, 1971)\n   100→- **Example:** (P ∨ Q) ∧ (¬P ∨ R) ∧ (¬Q ∨ ¬R)\n   101→\n   102→**2. 3-SAT**\n   103→- **Problem:** SAT restricted to formulas in conjunctive normal form with exactly 3 literals per clause\n   104→- **Status:** NP-complete (Karp, 1972)\n   105→- **Example:** (P ∨ Q ∨ R) ∧ (¬P ∨ Q ∨ ¬R) ∧ (P ∨ ¬Q ∨ S) ∧ (¬P ∨ ¬R ∨ ¬S)\n   106→\n   107→**3. Graph Problems**\n   108→- **Hamiltonian Cycle:** Does a graph have a cycle visiting each vertex exactly once?\n   109→- **Graph Coloring:** Can a graph be colored with k colors (k ≥ 3)?\n   110→- **Clique:** Does a graph contain a complete subgraph of size k?\n   111→- **Independent Set:** Does a graph have k vertices with no edges between them?\n   112→\n   113→**4. Optimization Problems**\n   114→- **Subset Sum:** Given integers, is there a subset summing to target T?\n   115→- **Knapsack:** Maximize value while staying under weight constraint\n   116→- **Traveling Salesman:** Find shortest tour visiting all cities\n   117→\n   118→**5. Scheduling and Packing**\n   119→- **Bin Packing:** Pack items into minimum number of bins\n   120→- **Job Scheduling:** Schedule jobs on machines to minimize completion time\n   121→\n   122→### 3.3 Problems Not Known to be in P or NP-Complete\n   123→\n   124→**Graph Isomorphism:**\n   125→- Determine if two graphs are structurally identical\n   126→- In NP but not known to be NP-complete or in P\n   127→- Recent quasi-polynomial time algorithm (Babai, 2015)\n   128→\n   129→**Integer Factorization:**\n   130→- Factor an integer into primes\n   131→- Associated decision problem Lfact is in NP ∩ coNP\n   132→- Believed not to be NP-complete\n   133→- Basis for RSA cryptography\n   134→\n   135→---\n   136→\n   137→## 4. Current State of Knowledge\n   138→\n   139→### 4.1 What We Know\n   140→\n   141→**Upper Bounds:**\n   142→- Best known SAT algorithms run in time ~O(1.5^n) for n variables\n   143→- No polynomial-time algorithm known for any NP-complete problem\n   144→- Many exponential and sub-exponential algorithms exist\n   145→\n   146→**Lower Bounds:**\n   147→- No super-linear lower bound proven for general Boolean circuits\n   148→- Best proven lower bound for explicit functions: ~4n gates\n   149→- Exponential lower bounds for restricted models (monotone circuits, bounded-depth circuits)\n   150→\n   151→**Complexity Class Relationships:**\n   152→```\n   153→LOGSPACE ⊆ P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXP\n   154→```\n   155→- We know LOGSPACE ⊊ PSPACE (by diagonalization)\n   156→- Cannot prove any adjacent inclusion is proper\n   157→- Believed that all inclusions are proper\n   158→\n   159→### 4.2 Known Barriers to Resolution\n   160→\n   161→**1. Relativization Barrier (Baker-Gill-Solovay, 1975)**\n   162→- There exist oracles A and B such that:\n   163→  - P^A = NP^A (relative to oracle A)\n   164→  - P^B ≠ NP^B (relative to oracle B)\n   165→- Implication: Techniques that relativize cannot resolve P vs NP\n   166→- Most classical proof techniques (diagonalization, simulation) relativize\n   167→\n   168→**2. Natural Proofs Barrier (Razborov-Rudich, 1997)**\n   169→- \"Natural proofs\" are constructive, large, and useful against P/poly\n   170→- If strong pseudo-random generators exist, natural proofs cannot prove circuit lower bounds\n   171→- Implication: Most known circuit lower bound techniques are blocked\n   172→\n   173→**3. Algebraic Barriers**\n   174→- Many algebraic techniques fail due to fundamental limitations\n   175→- Geometric complexity theory attempts to overcome this\n   176→\n   177→### 4.3 What Would Resolution Mean?\n   178→\n   179→**If P = NP:**\n   180→- Cryptography as we know it would collapse\n   181→- Optimization problems would become tractable\n   182→- Automated theorem proving would be practical\n   183→- Creative design could be automated\n   184→- However, polynomial might still be infeasible (e.g., n^1000)\n   185→\n   186→**If P ≠ NP:**\n   187→- Computational intractability is inherent to certain problems\n   188→- Cryptography has a solid foundation\n   189→- Optimization requires heuristics and approximations\n   190→- Supports current computational practice\n   191→\n   192→---\n   193→\n   194→## 5. Proof Approaches and Techniques\n   195→\n   196→### 5.1 Approaches for P = NP (Constructive)\n   197→\n   198→**Goal:** Exhibit a polynomial-time algorithm for an NP-complete problem\n   199→\n   200→**Standard Toolkit:**\n   201→- Greedy algorithms\n   202→- Dynamic programming\n   203→- Linear programming relaxations\n   204→- Divide and conquer\n   205→- Network flow techniques\n   206→\n   207→**Challenges:**\n   208→- 50+ years of attempts have failed\n   209→- Thousands of engineers and researchers have tried\n   210→- Industrial motivation extremely high\n   211→- Strong evidence against P = NP\n   212→\n   213→**Non-constructive Possibilities:**\n   214→- Robertson-Seymour type results (polynomial-time but infeasible)\n   215→- Non-uniform circuit families\n   216→\n   217→### 5.2 Approaches for P ≠ NP (Lower Bounds)\n   218→\n   219→**1. Diagonalization with Reduction**\n   220→- **Method:** Adapt techniques from computability theory\n   221→- **Success:** Super-exponential lower bounds for very hard problems (e.g., Presburger arithmetic)\n   222→- **Limitation:** Relativization barrier blocks application to P vs NP\n   223→\n   224→**2. Boolean Circuit Lower Bounds**\n   225→- **Goal:** Prove super-polynomial circuit size lower bound for NP-complete problem\n   226→- **Background:** Shannon (1949) proved almost all n-bit functions require 2^n/n gates\n   227→- **Progress:** Exponential lower bounds for restricted models:\n   228→  - Monotone circuits (Razborov, 1985)\n   229→  - Constant-depth circuits (Ajtai, 1983; Furst-Saxe-Sipser, 1984)\n   230→  - AC^0 circuits (Håstad, 1987)\n   231→- **Best General Result:** ~4n gates (far from super-polynomial)\n   232→- **Limitation:** Natural proofs barrier\n   233→\n   234→**3. Algebraic Techniques**\n   235→- **Method:** Represent Boolean functions as polynomials over finite fields\n   236→- **Success:** Lower bounds for arithmetic circuits\n   237→- **Example:** IP = PSPACE (Shamir, 1992) uses algebraic techniques\n   238→- **Advantage:** Can be non-relativizing\n   239→\n   240→**4. Geometric Complexity Theory (Mulmuley-Sohoni)**\n   241→- **Method:** Use algebraic geometry and representation theory\n   242→- **Goal:** Prove VP ≠ VNP (algebraic analogue of P vs NP)\n   243→- **Status:** Long-term research program, no resolution yet\n   244→\n   245→**5. Circuit Satisfiability Lower Bounds**\n   246→- **Williams' Approach (2010):** Convert algorithms into circuit lower bounds\n   247→- **Result:** NEXP ⊄ ACC^0\n   248→- **Significance:** First major non-relativizing separation in decades\n   249→- **Technique:** Combines algorithms, diagonalization, and circuit analysis\n   250→\n   251→### 5.3 Indirect Approaches\n   252→\n   253→**Proposition (Impagliazzo-Wigderson, 1997):**\n   254→- If some language in E (exponential time) requires exponential circuit size, then BPP = P\n   255→\n   256→**Proposition (Kabanets):**\n   257→- If every language in E has small circuits, then P ≠ NP\n   258→\n   259→**Implication:**\n   260→- Either we get derandomization (BPP = P) or we prove P ≠ NP\n   261→\n   262→---\n   263→\n   264→## 6. Related Complexity Classes\n   265→\n   266→### 6.1 coNP\n   267→- **Definition:** Complements of NP languages\n   268→- **Example:** TAUT (tautologies) is coNP-complete\n   269→- **Relationship:** If NP = coNP, then polynomial hierarchy collapses\n   270→- **Belief:** NP ≠ coNP (stronger than P ≠ NP)\n   271→\n   272→### 6.2 BPP (Bounded-Error Probabilistic Polynomial Time)\n   273→- **Definition:** Problems solvable by randomized algorithms with small error probability\n   274→- **Relationship:** P ⊆ BPP ⊆ PSPACE\n   275→- **Question:** Does BPP = P?\n   276→- **Belief:** BPP = P (derandomization conjecture)\n   277→\n   278→### 6.3 Polynomial Hierarchy\n   279→- **Definition:** Generalization of NP with alternating quantifiers\n   280→- **Levels:** Σ₁ᴾ = NP, Π₁ᴾ = coNP, Σ₂ᴾ, Π₂ᴾ, ...\n   281→- **Property:** If P = NP, hierarchy collapses to P\n   282→\n   283→### 6.4 PSPACE\n   284→- **Definition:** Problems solvable with polynomial space\n   285→- **Relationship:** NP ⊆ PSPACE\n   286→- **Question:** Does NP = PSPACE?\n   287→- **Belief:** NP ⊊ PSPACE\n   288→\n   289→### 6.5 Linear-Size Circuits\n   290→- **Definition:** LINEAR-SIZE = problems solvable by O(n)-size circuit families\n   291→- **Proposition:** If P ⊆ LINEAR-SIZE, then P ≠ NP\n   292→- **Belief:** P ⊄ LINEAR-SIZE\n   293→\n   294→---\n   295→\n   296→## 7. Computational Models\n   297→\n   298→### 7.1 Turing Machines\n   299→- **Standard Model:** Deterministic single-tape Turing machine\n   300→- **Robustness:** Multi-tape, random access variants all polynomial-time equivalent\n   301→- **Formal Definition:** See appendix of Clay Mathematics Institute problem description\n   302→\n   303→### 7.2 Boolean Circuits\n   304→- **Model:** Acyclic graph with AND, OR, NOT gates\n   305→- **Non-uniform:** Different circuit for each input length\n   306→- **Relationship:** P ⊆ P/poly (polynomial-size circuits)\n   307→- **Key Insight:** Circuit lower bounds sufficient for P ≠ NP\n   308→\n   309→### 7.3 Quantum Computers\n   310→- **Model:** Computation using quantum superposition\n   311→- **Known Results:** Shor's algorithm factors integers in polynomial time\n   312→- **Relationship to P vs NP:** Quantum computers likely don't solve NP-complete problems efficiently\n   313→- **Class:** BQP (Bounded-Error Quantum Polynomial Time)\n   314→- **Belief:** BQP incomparable to NP\n   315→\n   316→### 7.4 Randomized Algorithms\n   317→- **Model:** Algorithms with access to random bits\n   318→- **Classes:** RP, coRP, ZPP, BPP\n   319→- **Question:** Can randomness help solve NP-complete problems?\n   320→- **Belief:** No, but randomness useful for other problems\n   321→\n   322→---\n   323→\n   324→## 8. Practical Implications\n   325→\n   326→### 8.1 Current Practice\n   327→\n   328→**NP-Complete Problems in Industry:**\n   329→- **Approximation Algorithms:** Achieve near-optimal solutions (e.g., 2-approximation for vertex cover)\n   330→- **Heuristics:** Simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, greedy methods\n   331→- **SAT Solvers:** Highly optimized for practical instances (CDCL, DPLL)\n   332→- **Mixed Integer Programming:** Commercial solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi) effective on many real instances\n   333→- **Special Cases:** Identify tractable subclasses (e.g., 2-SAT in P, 3-SAT NP-complete)\n   334→\n   335→**Why Practice Differs from Worst-Case:**\n   336→- Real instances often have structure\n   337→- Average-case complexity may differ from worst-case\n   338→- Heuristics work well on practical data\n   339→\n   340→### 8.2 Average-Case Complexity\n   341→\n   342→**Levin's Theory:**\n   343→- Study problems hard on average, not just worst-case\n   344→- Average-case completeness\n   345→- Implications for cryptography\n   346→\n   347→**Smoothed Analysis:**\n   348→- Analyze algorithms on slightly perturbed inputs\n   349→- Explains why some algorithms work well in practice\n   350→\n   351→---\n   352→\n   353→## 9. Connection to Logic and Proof Theory\n   354→\n   355→### 9.1 Proof Complexity\n   356→\n   357→**Key Result (Cook-Reckhow, 1979):**\n   358→- NP ≠ coNP implies no propositional proof system has polynomial-size proofs for all tautologies\n   359→\n   360→**Implications:**\n   361→- Connects computational complexity to logic\n   362→- Motivates study of proof systems\n   363→\n   364→**Major Proof Systems:**\n   365→- Resolution\n   366→- Cutting planes\n   367→- Frege systems\n   368→- Extended Frege systems\n   369→\n   370→### 9.2 Independence Results\n   371→\n   372→**Potential Independence:**\n   373→- Some researchers speculate P vs NP might be independent of ZFC\n   374→- Would require going beyond standard axiomatization of mathematics\n   375→- No consensus on this possibility\n   376→\n   377→---\n   378→\n   379→## 10. Recent Developments (2015-2024)\n   380→\n   381→### Key Results\n   382→\n   383→**Graph Isomorphism (Babai, 2015):**\n   384→- Quasi-polynomial time algorithm\n   385→- Not polynomial, but major improvement\n   386→- Revised and corrected by 2017\n   387→\n   388→**Avi Wigderson (Turing Award, 2024):**\n   389→- Recognition of complexity theory contributions\n   390→- Continued importance of the field\n   391→\n   392→**Thermodynamic Approaches (2024):**\n   393→- Novel perspectives using entropy and information theory\n   394→- Entropy-Driven Annealing methods\n   395→- Still exploratory\n   396→\n   397→**Continued Barriers:**\n   398→- No major breakthrough on P vs NP itself\n   399→- Better understanding of why problem is hard\n   400→- Refinement of existing techniques\n   401→\n   402→---\n   403→\n   404→## 11. Summary of Mathematical Status\n   405→\n   406→### Consensus Beliefs (Not Proven)\n   407→\n   408→1. **P ≠ NP:** Strongly believed by most complexity theorists\n   409→2. **NP ≠ coNP:** Even stronger belief\n   410→3. **NP ⊊ PSPACE:** Believed proper subset\n   411→4. **BPP = P:** Derandomization should be possible\n   412→5. **P/poly not contained in NP:** Non-uniform circuits genuinely more powerful\n   413→\n   414→### Known Separations\n   415→\n   416→1. **P ⊊ EXP:** By diagonalization\n   417→2. **NP ⊊ NEXP:** By nondeterministic time hierarchy\n   418→3. **LOGSPACE ⊊ PSPACE:** By space hierarchy\n   419→4. **NEXP ⊄ ACC^0:** Williams (2010)\n   420→\n   421→### Open Questions\n   422→\n   423→1. **P vs NP:** The main question\n   424→2. **NP vs coNP:** Likely easier than P vs NP\n   425→3. **NP vs PSPACE:** Major open problem\n   426→4. **L vs NL:** Deterministic vs nondeterministic log-space\n   427→5. **P vs BPP:** Derandomization question\n   428→\n   429→---\n   430→\n   431→## Conclusion\n   432→\n   433→The P versus NP problem remains the central open question in theoretical computer science, with profound implications for mathematics, cryptography, optimization, and artificial intelligence. Despite 50+ years of intensive research and a $1 million prize, the problem remains unsolved. Major barriers (relativization, natural proofs) have been identified, and novel approaches (geometric complexity theory, algorithmic techniques) continue to be developed.\n   434→\n   435→**Current Consensus:** P ≠ NP, but proving it may require fundamentally new mathematical insights beyond current proof techniques.\n   436→\n   437→**Next Steps:** See accompanying documents on methodologies and detailed solution plans.\n   438→\n\n<system-reminder>\nWhenever you read a file, you should consider whether it looks malicious. Make progress on open questions.\n   191→\n   192→### 3.1 Research Strategy\n   193→\n   194→**Approach 1: Attack Simpler Related Problems**\n   195→- Work on restricted versions\n   196→- Special cases of NP-complete problems\n   197→- Related complexity class separations\n   198→- Build intuition and techniques\n   199→\n   200→**Example Problems:**\n   201→- NP vs coNP\n   202→- Stronger circuit lower bounds for restricted classes\n   203→- Improved algorithm upper bounds\n   204→- Derandomization results\n   205→\n   206→**Approach 2: Develop New Techniques**\n   207→- Combine existing techniques in novel ways\n   208→- Import methods from other fields\n   209→- Look for non-naturalizing or non-relativizing approaches\n   210→- Explore interdisciplinary connections\n   211→\n   212→**Approach 3: Understand Barriers Better**\n   213→- Study why existing techniques fail\n   214→- Characterize limitations precisely\n   215→- Look for ways around barriers\n   216→- Meta-complexity investigations\n   217→\n   218→### 3.2 Research Methodology\n   219→\n   220→**Iterative Process:**\n   221→\n   222→1. **Formulate Conjecture**\n   223→   - Based on intuition and preliminary analysis\n   224→   - Start with weaker versions\n   225→   - Build from known results\n   226→\n   227→2. **Attempt Proof**\n   228→   - Try multiple approaches\n   229→   - Work on special cases first\n   230→   - Look for counterexamples if appropriate\n   231→   - Document all attempts\n   232→\n   233→3. **Analyze Obstacles**\n   234→   - Identify where proof breaks down\n   235→   - Theoretical Foundations\n    10→\n    11→### 1.1 Computational Models\n    12→\n    13→**Turing Machines**\n    14→- **Purpose:** Formal model of computation; standard for defining P and NP\n    15→- **Variants:**\n    16→  - Single-tape deterministic Turing machine (DTM)\n    17→  - Multi-tape Turing machine\n    18→  - Nondeterministic Turing machine (NTM)\n    19→  - Oracle Turing machine\n    20→  - Alternating Turing machine\n    21→- **Tools for Analysis:**\n    22→  - Gates: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR\n    34→  - Unbounded fan-in variants\n    35→  - Special gates: MOD, MAJORITY, THRESHOLD\n    36→- **Measures:**\n    37→  - Size: Number of gates\n    38→  - Depth: Longest path from input to output\n    39→  - Width: Maximum number of gates at any level\n    40→- **Circuit Classes:**\n    41→  - NC: Polylog depth, polynomial size\n    42→  - AC^0: Constant depth, unbounded fan-in AND/OR\n    43→  - TC^0: AC^0 plus MAJORITY gates\n    44→  - ACC^0: AC^0 plus MOD gates\n    45→- **Tools:**\n    46→  - Circuit simulators\n    47→  - Circuit complexity libraries\n    48→\n    49→**Boolean Functions**\n    50→- **Representations:**\n    51→  - Circuit complexity\n    57→  - Formula size\n    58→  - Decision tree complexity\n    59→  - Communication complexity\n    60→  - Polynomial degree\n    61→\n    62→### 1.2 Complexity Classes\n    63→\n    64→**Resource-Bounded Classes**\n    65→- **Time-Bounded:**\n    66→  - DTIME(f(n)): Deterministic time f(n)\n    67→  - NTIME(f(n)): Nondeterministic time f(n)\n    68→  - P = ⋃ₖ DTIME(n^k)\n    69→  - NP = ⋃ₖ NTIME(n^k)\n    70→  - EXP, NEXP, 2-EXP\n    71→- **Space-Bounded:**\n    72→  - Approximation algorithms\n   244→  - Smoothed analysis\n   245→- **Techniques:**\n   246→  - Fourier analysis\n   247→  - Harmonic analysis\n   248→  - Approximation theory\n   249→\n   250→**Algebraic Geometry**\n   251→- **Applications:**\n   252→  - Geometric complexity theory (GCT)\n   253→  - Valiant's algebraic complexity classes\n   254→- **Concepts:**\n   255→  - Varieties and ideals\n   256→  - Orbit closures\n   257→  - Representation-theoretic obstructions\n   258→- **Tools:**\n   259→  - Macaulay2\n   260→  - Singular\n   261→  - CoCoA\n   262→\n   263→---\n   264→\n   265→## 3. Proof Techniques\n   266→\n   267→### 3.1 Classical Techniques\n   268→\n   269→**Diagonalization**\n   270→- **Method:** Construct problem that differs from all polynomial-time algorithms\n   271→- **Applications:**\n   272→  - Time hierarchy theorem\n   273→  - Space hierarchy theorem\n   274→  - P ⊊ EXP\n   275→- **Limitation:** Relativization barrier for P vs NP\n   276→- **Tools:**\n   277→  - Enumeration of Turing machines\n   278→  - Universal Turing machine constructions\n   279→\n   280→**Simulation and Reduction**\n   281→- **Types:**\n   282→  - Many-one reductions (≤ₘ)\n   283→  - Turing reductions (≤T)\n   284→  - Polynomial-time reductions (≤p)\n   285→  - Log-space reductions (≤L)\n   286→- **Applications:**\n   287→  - Proving NP-completeness\n   288→  - Class inclusions\n   289→- **Technique:** Show L₁ ≤p L₂ and L₂ ∈ P implies L₁ ∈ P\n   290→\n   291→**Padding Arguments**\n   292→- **Method:** Scale problem instances to relate classes at different time bounds\n   293→- **Applications:**\n   294→  - Relating P vs NP to other separations\n   295→  - Downward separations\n   296→\n   297→### 3.2 Circuit Lower Bounds\n   298→\n   299→**Monotone Circuit Lower Bounds**\n   300→- **Method:** Analyze circuits without NOT gates\n   301→- **Key Result:** Razborov (1985) - monotone circuit for CLIQUE requires exponential size\n   302→- **Technique:** Approximation method\n   303→- **Limitation:** Doesn't apply to general circuits\n   304→\n   305→**Constant-Depth Circuit Lower Bounds**\n   306→- **Ajtai (1983), Furst-Saxe-Sipser (1984):**\n   307→  - PARITY not in AC^0\n   308→  - Method: Switching lemma, random restrictions\n   309→- **Håstad (1987):**\n   310→  - Optimal AC^0 lower bounds\n   311→  - Refined switching lemma\n   312→- **Razborov-Smolensky (1987):**\n   313→  - ACC^0 lower bounds for MOD functions\n   314→  - Method: Polynomial approximation\n   315→\n   316→**Communication Complexity Lower Bounds**\n   317→- **Method:** Study communication required for distributed computation\n   318→- **Applications:**\n   319→  - Circuit depth lower bounds\n   320→  - Streaming algorithms\n   321→  - Data structure lower bounds\n   322→- **Techniques:**\n   323→  - Fooling sets\n   324→  - Rank arguments\n   325→  - Discrepancy method\n   326→  - Information complexity\n   327→\n   328→**Algebraic Methods**\n   329→- **Polynomial Degree Bounds:**\n   330→  - Lower bound degree of polynomial representing function\n   331→- **Arithmetic Circuit Lower Bounds:**\n   332→  - VP vs VNP (Valiant's classes)\n   333→  - Permanent vs determinant\n   334→\n   335→### 3.3 Algorithm Design Implies Lower Bounds\n   336→\n   337→**Williams' Technique (2010)**\n   338→- **Insight:** Better algorithms for circuit satisfiability imply circuit lower bounds\n   339→- **Result:** NEXP ⊄ ACC^0\n   340→- **Method:**\n   341→  1. Design fast satisfiability algorithm for circuit class C\n   342→  2. Use algorithm in diagonalization\n   343→  3. Conclude NEXP or NEXP/poly not in C\n   344→- **Significance:** First major non-relativizing separation in decades\n   345→\n   346→**Tools for Implementation:**\n   347→- Algorithm analysis\n   348→- Satisfiability algorithms\n   349→- Derandomization techniques\n   350→\n   351→### 3.4 Natural Proofs and Barriers\n   352→\n   353→**Natural Proofs Framework (Razborov-Rudich, 1997)**\n   354→- **Properties of Natural Proofs:**\n   355→  1. **Constructivity:** Can efficiently recognize \"hard\" functions\n   356→  2. **Largeness:** Many functions satisfy the property\n   357→  3. **Usefulness:** Property implies super-polynomial lower bounds\n   358→- **Barrier:** If strong PRGs exist, natural proofs can't prove P/poly lower bounds\n   359→- **Implication:** Need non-natural techniques\n   360→\n   361→**Overcoming Barriers:**\n   362→- Non-relativizing techniques (arithmetization, algebraic methods)\n   363→- Non-naturalizing techniques (specific structure, non-uniformity gaps)\n   364→- Algorithm-to-lower-bound connections (Williams' approach)\n   365→\n   366→### 3.5 Indirect and Structural Approaches\n   367→\n   368→**Polynomial Hierarchy Collapse**\n   369→- **Strategy:** Show P = NP implies unexpected consequences\n   370→- **Example:** If P = NP, then PH collapses to P\n   371→\n   372→**Average-Case vs Worst-Case**\n   373→- **Approach:** Study average-case complexity\n   374→- **Tools:**\n   375→  - Levin's average-case completeness\n   376→  - Hardness amplification\n   377→  - Worst-case to average-case reductions\n   378→\n   379→**Cryptographic Approaches**\n   380→- **Insight:** Cryptographic hardness assumptions related to P vs NP\n   381→- **Tools:**\n   382→  - One-way functions\n   383→  - Pseudorandom generators\n   384→  - Hardness assumptions\n   385→\n   386→---\n   387→\n   388→## 4. Computational Tools\n   389→\n   390→### 4.1 SAT Solvers\n   391→\n   392→**Modern CDCL Solvers**\n   393→- **Examples:** MiniSat, CryptoMiniSat, Glucose, Lingeling\n   394→- **Features:**\n   395→  - Conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL)\n   396→  - Watched literals\n   397→  - Restart strategies\n   398→  - Clause deletion\n   399→- **Use Cases:**\n   400→  - Solving practical SAT instances\n   401→  - Specific Research Programs\n   604→\n   605→### 6.1 Geometric Complexity Theory (GCT)\n   606→\n   607→**Goals:**\n   608→- Prove P ≠ NP or VP ≠ VNP via algebraic geometry\n   609→- Use representation theory and orbit closures\n   610→\n   611→**Key Concepts:**\n   612→- **Orbit closures:** Geometric objects representing complexity\n   613→- **Representation-theoretic obstructions:** Barriers to simulation\n   614→- **Mulmuley-Sohoni program:** Long-term research agenda\n   615→\n   616→**Tools:**\n   617→- Algebraic geometry (Macaulay2, Singular)\n   618→- Representation theory (GAP, Sage)\n   619→- Group theory\n   620→\n   621→**Status:**\n   622→- Long-term program\n   623→- Partial results on representation-theoretic barriers\n   624→- Full resolution not yet achieved\n   625→\n   626→**Resources:**\n   627→- Mulmuley's papers and lectures\n   628→- GCT workshop proceedings\n   629→\n   630→### 6.2 Proof Complexity\n   631→\n   632→**Goals:**\n   633→- Understand propositional proof systems\n   634→- Connect to NP vs coNP\n   635→\n   636→**Key Result:**\n   637→- If NP ≠ coNP, no proof system has polynomial-size proofs for all tautologies\n   638→\n   639→**Research Areas:**\n   640→- Lower bounds for resolution\n   641→- Frege system analysis\n   642→- Extended Frege systems\n   643→- Algebraic proof systems (IPS)\n   644→\n   645→**Tools:**\n   646→- Proof complexity libraries\n   647→- Automated proof generation\n   648→\n   649→**Resources:**\n   650→- Krajíček's \"Proof Complexity\"\n   651→- Recent papers in CCC, STOC, FOCS\n   652→\n   653→### 6.3 Derandomization\n   654→\n   655→**Goal:**\n   656→- Prove BPP = P\n   657→- Eliminate randomness from algorithms\n   658→\n   659→**Approaches:**\n   660→- **Pseudorandom generators:**\n   661→  - Construct PRGs from hard functions\n   662→  - Impagliazzo-Wigderson framework\n   663→- **Hardness vs randomness:**\n   664→  - Hard functions imply derandomization\n   665→\n   666→**Connection to P vs NP:**\n   667→- If E requires exponential circuits, then BPP = P\n   668→- If E has small circuits, then P ≠ NP (Kabanets)\n   669→\n   670→**Tools:**\n   671→- PRG implementations\n   672→- Hardness amplification techniques\n   673→\n   674→### 6.4 Fine-Grained Complexity\n   675→\n   676→**Goal:**\n   677→- Understand relationships within P\n   678→- Classify problems by best possible running time\n   679→\n   680→**Key Hypotheses:**\n   681→- **Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH):** SAT requires 2^n time\n   682→- **3SUM hypothesis**\n   683→- **APSP hypothesis**\n   684→\n   685→**Method:**\n   686→- Conditional lower bounds based on conjectures\n   687→- Fine-grained reductions\n   688→\n   689→**Relevance:**\n   690→- Understanding structure within P\n   691→- Practical algorithm design\n   692→\n   693→---\n   694→\n   695→## 7. Logs the limit reached message\n2. Closes the application modal\n3. Waits 1 hour (3600 seconds)\n4. Refreshes the page to the target URL\n5. Continues the automation loop to retry\n\n## Changes\n\n### Files Modified\n- **playwright-click-and-type.js**: Added textarea check and limit detection logic\n- **puppeteer-click-and-type.js**: Added textarea check and limit detection logic\n\n### Implementation Details\n\n**Textarea Empty Check** (both files):\n```javascript\n// Issue #47 Fix 1: Only type if textarea is empty to prevent double typing\nconst currentValue = await textarea.inputValue(); // or el.value for Puppeteer\nif (!currentValue || currentValue.trim() === '') {\n  await textarea.type(MESSAGE);\n  console.log('✅ typed message successfully');\n} else {\n  console.log('⏭️  textarea already contains text, skipping typing to prevent double entry');\n}\n```\n\n**Limit Detection** (both files):\n```javascript\n// Issue #47 Fix 2: Check for 200 application limit error\nconst limitErrorSelector = '[data-qa-popup-error-code=\"negotiations-limit-exceeded\"]';\nconst limitError = page.locator(limitErrorSelector);\nconst hasLimitError = await limitError.count() > 0;\n\nif (hasLimitError) {\n  console.log('⚠️  Limit reached: 200 applications in 24 hours');\n  console.log('💤 Waiting 1 hour before retrying...');\n  \n  // Close modal, wait 1 hour, refresh page, and retry\n  // ... (implementation details in code)\n}\n```\n\n## Testing\n\n- ✅ All syntax checks pass (`npm run check`)\n- ✅ ESLint passes (`npm run lint`)\n- ✅ Both Playwright and Puppeteer implementations updated consistently\n\n## Benefits\n\n- **Prevents duplicate messages**: Employers will receive clean, single-instance cover letters\n- **Handles rate limiting gracefully**: Script waits appropriately when limit is reached instead of failing\n- **Automatic retry**: After waiting period, script refreshes and continues processing applications\n- **Better user experience**: Clear console logging shows what's happening at each step\n\n## Code Locations\n\n- `playwright-click-and-type.js:266-292` - Limit detection logic\n- `playwright-click-and-type.js:297-306` - Textarea empty check\n- `puppeteer-click-and-type.js:264-289` - Limit detection logic  \n- `puppeteer-click-and-type.js:300-309` - Textarea empty check\n\nFixes #47\n\n---\n\n🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>",

Added a new `_needs_websocket_param()` function that checks if any `FromDishka` dependencies are of type `WebSocket`\n2. Created a new `DISHKA_WEBSOCKET_PARAM` synthetic parameter (in addition to the existing `DISHKA_REQUEST_PARAM`)\n3. Modified `_wrap_fastapi_injection()` to choose the appropriate synthetic parameter:\n   - If the function has `FromDishka[WebSocket]` dependencies, add `___dishka_websocket: WebSocket`\n   - Otherwise, add `___dishka_request: Request`\n4. When no plain `Request` or `WebSocket` parameter was found, the code would add a synthetic `___dishka_request` parameter of type `Request`\n2. Created a new `DISHKA_WEBSOCKET_PARAM` synthetic parameter (in addition to the existing `DISHKA_REQUEST_PARAM`)\n3. Modified `_wrap_fastapi_injection()` to choose the appropriate synthetic parameter:\n   - If the function has `FromDishka[WebSocket]` dependencies, add `___dishka_websocket: WebSocket`\n   - Otherwise, add `___dishka_request: Request`\n4. This is a known issue documented in the Changesets GitHub repository.\n\n### The Solution\n\nRunning `npm install` ensures that the version is updated in the package-lock.json file after running `changeset version`. This does not appear to have any ill effect and may be purely cosmetic.\n\n### Similar Issue with pnpm\n\nThis same problem exists with pnpm as well. When using pnpm with changesets in a monorepo, after merging the \"Update Versions\" PR from the changesets action, CI breaks on the \"Install\" step since changesets has updated the versions in linked packages but has not updated the pnpm-lock.yaml.\n\n### How npm Handles package-lock.json Updates\n\npackage-lock.json is automatically generated for any operations where npm modifies either the node_modules tree, or package.json. It describes the exact tree that was generated, such that subsequent installs are able to generate identical trees, regardless of intermediate dependency updates.\n\n### Best Practice\n\nAfter running `changeset version` to bump your package versions, you should run `npm install` to ensure the package-lock.json file is updated to reflect the new versions."
